title: 3Sum Closest
interviewTips: Clarify: n >= 3 guaranteed? Return sum value not indices? What to do on exact match vs closest? Is tie-breaking needed?
Trade-off: Brute force O(n^3) needs no sorting but fails for n=1000; sorting O(n log n) enables O(n^2) two-pointers which is optimal for comparison-based 3Sum variants.
Edge-case tip: Initialize closest with first triplet, early-exit when sum == target, and use long or careful abs to avoid overflow if constraints grow.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Enumeration
approaches.intuition: Try every triplet i<j<k and keep the sum with minimal absolute difference to target. Simplest first-principles baseline that is always correct.
approaches.theory: Enumerate all C(n,3) combinations with three nested loops. Maintain best variable closest, updating when abs(s-target) < abs(closest-target). No sorting or pruning needed. Correct because search space is exhaustive.

timeComplexity.explanation: Three nested loops enumerate all O(n^3) triplets, each O(1) sum and compare.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only constant extra variables for indices, sum and closest.

edgeCases: n==3: only one triplet, return its sum directly
Exact match exists: should return target immediately
All negative or all positive with far target: diff logic still works
Duplicate values: enumeration handles them without special logic

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sorting + Binary Search
approaches.intuition: Sort the array, fix first two numbers, then the ideal third value is determined: need = target - a - b. Find closest to need in the suffix with binary search.
approaches.theory: After sorting, for each pair (i,j) the function f(k)=nums[i]+nums[j]+nums[k] is monotonic in k. So closest k to need can be found via lower_bound in O(log n). Check both lower_bound index and its predecessor because closest may be on either side. Overall O(n^2 log n) after O(n log n) sort.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting O(n log n) plus O(n^2) pairs each with O(log n) binary search.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In-place sort aside, only O(1) extra; sort stack may be O(log n).

steps: i=0(-4), j=1(-1): need=6, lower_bound in [1,2] -> end, check 2: s=-3 diff 4 -> closest=-3
i=0(-4), j=2(1): need=4, idx->end, check 2: s=-1 diff 2 -> closest=-1
i=1(-1), j=2(1): need=1, idx=2(val 1): s=1 diff 0? Actually -1+1+1=1 diff 0 -> closest=1? Wait duplicate use? No, idx=2 is j itself? lo=j+1=3 so idx=3(val 2): s=2 diff 1 -> closest=2

edgeCases: need smaller than all suffix values: lower_bound returns j+1, only check idx
need larger than all suffix values: lower_bound returns n, only check idx-1
n==3: inner loops run once, binary search range size 1

approaches.name: Approach 3: Sorting + Two Pointers
approaches.intuition: Sort, fix i, then use left/right pointers to converge on target: if sum is too small move left right, if too large move right left, tracking best along the way.
approaches.theory: For fixed i, the 2Sum-closest subproblem on sorted suffix is solvable linearly with two pointers because monotonicity lets us discard one side per step. If s < target, any pair with same left and smaller right is even smaller, so increment left; symmetrically decrement right if s > target. Scanning all i gives global optimum in O(n^2).

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting O(n log n) plus outer loop n times with linear two-pointer scan O(n) each, total O(n^2) dominant.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In-place sort plus O(1) pointers and best variable; sort recursion O(log n) in some languages.

edgeCases: n==3: single i iteration, one sum evaluated
target far outside achievable range: pointers sweep to one end, closest is min or max sum
All duplicates e.g. [0,0,0]: pointers still converge, early exit if target 0
Overflow concern: with given limits int safe; use long if limits expanded
